--- title: "Monte Carlo: Applying It, Justifying It" subtitle: "Lecture 09" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "September 28, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## Last Class, In Two Formulas $$\tilde\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \quad\text{is unbiased,}\qquad \tilde\sigma_n = \frac{\sigma_Y}{\sqrt{n}} \quad\text{is its standard error.}$$ ::: {.fragment .fade-in} And a 95% confidence interval: $\tilde\mu_n \pm 1.96\,\sigma_Y/\sqrt{n}$. **We still owe an answer** to the DO ensemble question from a few classes ago: how many runs would we trust? Today: the actual answer, and how to justify it on your own work. ::: ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # Back to the River ## Framing the DO Question as Monte Carlo Recall Streeter-Phelps: the incoming CBOD load $B_0$ varies day to day, $B_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(9, 1.5^2)$ mg/L. **What is the probability that the minimum DO falls below the 2.5 mg/L standard on a randomly chosen day?** ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} do_params = let ka, kc, kn = 0.6, 0.4, 0.25 C0, N0, Cs, U = 6.2, 7.0, 7.0, 5.0 L = 40.0 standard = 2.5 (; ka, kc, kn, C0, N0, Cs, U, L, standard) end function do_min(B0, params; dx=0.1) steps = Int(round(params.L / dx)) C = params.C0 m = C for i in 1:steps x = (i - 1) * dx C = C + dx * ((params.ka * (params.Cs - C) - params.kc * B0 * exp(-params.kc * x / params.U) - params.kn * params.N0 * exp(-params.kn * x / params.U)) / params.U) m = min(m, C) end return m end violates(params) = do_min(max(0.1, rand(Normal(9.0, 1.5))), params) < params.standard ``` ::: ## Watching the Estimate Settle ::: {#cell-fig-mc-do .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} Random.seed!(4750) N = 20_000 draws = [violates(do_params) for _ in 1:N] running_p = cumsum(draws) ./ (1:N) running_se = zeros(N) running_se[1] = NaN for i in 2:N running_se[i] = sqrt(running_p[i] * (1 - running_p[i]) / i) end p_mc = plot(1:N, running_p, ribbon=1.96 .* running_se, xscale=:log10, color=:black, linewidth=3, fillalpha=0.25, fillcolor=cb_blue, xlabel="Number of samples n", ylabel="P(violation)", legend=false, ylims=(0, 1)) hline!(p_mc, [running_p[end]], color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2) plot!(p_mc, size=(1100, 460), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-mc-do .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Running Monte Carlo estimate of P(violation), with its 95% confidence band. ::: ::: ## The Number, With Honesty About Its Uncertainty | $n$ | estimate | 95% CI | |---:|---:|:---| | $5$ | $0.6$ | $[0.17, 1.03]$ | | $20$ | $0.4$ | $[0.19, 0.61]$ | | $100$ | $0.44$ | $[0.34, 0.54]$ | | $500$ | $0.47$ | $[0.43, 0.52]$ | | $2000$ | $0.45$ | $[0.43, 0.48]$ | | $20000$ | $0.46$ | $[0.45, 0.47]$ | ::: {.fragment .fade-in} **At $n=5$ the interval spans nearly the whole unit range** --- it can't even rule out "the river always violates" or "never does." That is exactly the five runs Streeter-Phelps used to pose the question. They were not enough to trust. ::: # Justifying a Sample Size ## The Rubric You Will Be Graded On ::: {.quote} > +2 for justification of Monte Carlo sample size. **Deadly Sin: No points will be given for a Monte Carlo solution with an arbitrary sample size.** +2 for an estimate of the Monte Carlo standard error. +1 for setting a seed for reproducibility. ::: {.cite} --- the Monte Carlo Rubric, `policies/rubric.qmd` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This is the **same discipline as $\Delta t$ in Week 4**, with $n$ in place of the step size: ::: ## The Same Discipline, a Different Knob :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} **Simulation** (Week 4) - pick $\Delta t$ from a characteristic timescale - halve it; see if the answer moves - error $\sim \Delta t$ ::: ::: {.column width=50%} **Monte Carlo** (today) - pick $n$ from a target CI half-width - double it; see if the estimate moves - error $\sim 1/\sqrt{n}$ ::: :::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Both times: name a quantity of interest, refine the knob, estimate what's left, **report what you did**. Both rubrics penalize not doing it. ::: ## The Sentence You Copy Into Your Homework > "I estimated $P(\text{DO} < 2.5\ \text{mg/L})$ with $n = 2{,}000$ Monte Carlo samples, seeded for reproducibility. The estimate is $0.454$ with a Monte Carlo standard error of $0.0111$, giving a 95% CI of $[0.43, 0.48]$. Doubling to $n=4{,}000$ changed the estimate by $0.003$ --- less than the standard error --- so $n=2{,}000$ is sufficient for this analysis." # Two Errors, One Answer ## You Now Have Two Knobs Every number you report from this model is shaped by two choices you made: ::: {.incremental} - $\Delta x$, the spatial step --- Week 4's knob. - $n$, the number of samples --- today's. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Refining either one costs time. **Which should you refine?** ::: ## Put Them in the Same Units The two errors are not comparable until they describe the same quantity. So express both as an error in **the violation probability**, which is the number you would actually report. - **Grid error**: hold $n$ and the seed fixed, vary $\Delta x$, see how $P$ moves. - **Sampling error**: hold $\Delta x$ fixed, and read the half-width $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. ## Measuring the Grid Error ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function violation_fraction(grid_step, sample_count, seed) Random.seed!(seed) violations = 0 for _ in 1:sample_count load = max(0.1, rand(Normal(9.0, 1.5))) if do_min(load, do_params; dx=grid_step) < do_params.standard violations += 1 end end return violations / sample_count end grid_steps = [1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1] reference_p = violation_fraction(0.02, 3000, 99) grid_estimates = zeros(length(grid_steps)) for i in 1:length(grid_steps) grid_estimates[i] = violation_fraction(grid_steps[i], 3000, 99) end grid_errors = abs.(grid_estimates .- reference_p) ``` ::: | $\Delta x$ (km) | $P$ | error vs. fine grid | |---:|---:|---:| | $1.0$ | $0.663$ | $0.201$ | | $0.5$ | $0.562$ | $0.1$ | | $0.25$ | $0.512$ | $0.05$ | | $0.1$ | $0.482$ | $0.02$ | ## Measuring the Sampling Error | $n$ | 95% half-width | |---:|---:| | $100$ | $0.098$ | | $500$ | $0.044$ | | $2000$ | $0.022$ | | $8000$ | $0.011$ | ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Sampling error falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$ --- predictably, and as slowly as we warned on Wednesday. ::: ## Two Errors, Two Rates ::: {#cell-fig-two-rates .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Sampling error measured against this chain's own long-run estimate. # The sampling error we plot is the half-width we would actually report, not # one chain's realised error -- a single chain's error is itself random and # does not fall smoothly. sample_sizes = [50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10_000] sampling_errors = zeros(length(sample_sizes)) for i in 1:length(sample_sizes) sampling_errors[i] = 1.96 * sqrt(reference_p * (1 - reference_p) / sample_sizes[i]) end p_grid = plot(grid_steps, grid_errors, xscale=:log10, yscale=:log10, markershape=:circle, markersize=7, color=cb_vermillion, linewidth=3, xlabel="Δx [km]", ylabel="error in P", label="measured", legend=:bottomright, xticks=(grid_steps, string.(grid_steps))) plot!(p_grid, grid_steps, grid_errors[1] .* (grid_steps ./ grid_steps[1]), color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="slope 1") p_samp = plot(sample_sizes, sampling_errors, xscale=:log10, yscale=:log10, markershape=:circle, markersize=7, color=cb_blue, linewidth=3, xlabel="n", ylabel="95% half-width in P", label="reported", legend=:bottomleft) plot!(p_samp, sample_sizes, sampling_errors[1] .* sqrt.(sample_sizes[1] ./ sample_sizes), color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash, label="slope -1/2") plot(p_grid, p_samp, layout=(1, 2), size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-two-rates .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Left: measured grid error against step size, with a slope-1 reference. Right: the reported 95% half-width against sample count, with a slope -1/2 reference. Both on log-log axes. ::: ::: ## One You Measure, One You Predict Note what had to be done to get each panel. ::: {.incremental} - **Grid error**: there is no formula. You found it by *refining and comparing* --- the same thing Week 4 made you do. - **Sampling error**: you can write it down **before running anything**, from $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} That asymmetry is why the grid error is the one people skip. Nothing prompts you to look for it, and no formula hands it to you. ::: ## Which One Dominates? At $\Delta x = 1$ km and $n = 2{,}000$ --- both perfectly reasonable-looking choices --- the grid error is **9\.2 times** the sampling half-width. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Refining $n$ here buys you almost nothing. The answer is limited by the grid, not the samples. ::: ## The Error You Can See Your confidence interval is computed from $n$ alone. **It knows nothing about $\Delta x$.** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} So a report that says $P = 0.30 \pm 0.02$ is quoting a precise answer to a model that has not been resolved. The interval is honest about the error it measures and silent about the one that dominates. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} **Report both, or the interval misleads.** ::: # From Probability to Risk ## You Have a Number. Is It Risk? We estimated the probability that dissolved oxygen falls below the standard on a given day. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} That is a real and useful number. It is also **not** a risk estimate. ::: ## What Risk Means The [*Society for Risk Analysis* definition](https://www.sra.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/SRA-Glossary-FINAL.pdf): ::: {.quote} > "risk" involves uncertainty about the effects/implications of an activity with respect to something that humans value (such as health, well-being, wealth, property or the environment), often focusing on negative, undesirable consequences. ::: ## Risk Is Not Probability **"Risk" is not just another word for probability.** It involves: ::: {.incremental} - uncertainty; - *undesirable* outcomes; - **effects**, not just the events themselves. ::: ## Components of Risk :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} Several things combine to produce risk: - Probability of a **hazard**; - **Exposure** to that hazard; - **Vulnerability** to the outcomes; - Socioeconomic **responses**. ::: ::: {.column width=50%} ![Overview of the Components of Risk](figures/simpson_risk.svg) ::: {.caption} Source: [Simpson et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oneear.2021.03.005) ::: ::: :::: ## Our Model Contains One of Four $P(\text{DO} < 2.5)$ is a **hazard** statistic, and nothing more. ::: {.incremental} - Who is **exposed**? Which reach, whose water intake, which fishery? - How **vulnerable** are they? A brief dip matters differently to a trout stream than to an industrial intake. - What is the **response**? A warning system, a permit change, a treatment upgrade. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} None of those three are in the model. **Managing risk needs all four, and simulation gives you one.** ::: # Practical Notes ## Pseudorandomness and Seeds :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=40%} Random number generators are not *really* random --- only **pseudorandom**, and deterministic given a seed. **Always set a seed.** It's how your results (and your grader's) reproduce. ::: ::: {.column width=60%} ![XKCD 221: Random Number](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/random_number.png){width=90%} ::: {.caption} Source: [XKCD #221](https://xkcd.com/221/) ::: ::: :::: # Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule ## Key Takeaways ::: {.incremental} - **Sample size needs justification**, exactly like Week 4's step size: pick $n$ from a target precision, double it and check, report the standard error. - Five samples were nowhere near enough to trust the DO ensemble --- now you know how to say precisely how far short they fell. - **Two errors sit in every answer**, and they fall at different rates. Refining the wrong knob buys nothing. - **Your confidence interval measures one of them and is silent about the other.** - A violation probability is a **hazard** statistic. Risk needs exposure, vulnerability, and response as well --- and none of those is in the model. ::: ## Next Classes **Wednesday**: Gaussian plumes --- deriving the model, boundary conditions, and where the closed form comes from. ## Assessments **Mini-Project 1**: Due Thursday, October 8. **Homework 4**: Assigned Wednesday, due Thursday, October 8. **Quiz 2**: Wednesday, covering discretization, convergence, Streeter-Phelps, and Monte Carlo foundations. # References ## References
